items.title: Democrats take Congress, but America's tariffs are likely to stay
items.summary: The midterm result with the legal reasons tariffs survive, plus the tariff diagram. Replaces the 1 November pre-vote forecast.
items.lede: Voters punished President Trump over the cost of living, with Democrats winning both houses on 3 November, but trade lawyers say the tariff wall will not come down because the powers now used do not need Congress each year. A bill to roll tariffs back could be vetoed, and overriding a veto needs two-thirds of the Senate.
items.angle: Use the midterms as evidence that protection has political as well as economic costs, then explain why tariffs persist: legal authority (Sections 122, 232, 301 and, for the first time, 338), the veto and bipartisan support on China. Expect hearings and oversight rather than repeal.
items.note: Replaces the 1 November forecast item, which gave the pre-election Congress as House 218-214 and Senate 53-47 (Republican majorities), a 10% temporary global tariff, about 20 trade deals claimed by the White House and a probe into 16 partners. The counts here are early and some seats were still to be called. Advisers say firms should plan for tariffs staying high and expect a push for tighter chip and AI export controls.

items.title: China extends its US tariff truce by two months
items.summary: A live US-China trade truce that keeps a tariff from rising, shown on a tariff diagram, though a two-month horizon leaves traders uncertain.
items.lede: Bloomberg reports that China has extended its pause on US tariffs and trade curbs for another two months. The article is paywalled, so only the headline and web address were read; the address indicates that the extra 24% tariff on US goods stays suspended until January and the 10% rate stays in place.
items.angle: Background: in November 2025 China suspended the extra 24% tariff for one year from 10 November 2025 and kept a 10% tariff on US goods, while the US cut its extra tariff on Chinese goods from 20% to 10% and China lifted some tariffs on US farm goods such as soybeans. On a tariff diagram a tariff lifts the domestic price from Pw to Pw+t, raises domestic output, cuts consumption and imports, and raises government revenue, with deadweight losses; if the truce lapsed the tariff would rise and these effects would grow. A two-month extension avoids a tariff jump for now but leaves traders with a short planning horizon.
items.note: Paywalled: only the headline and web address were read, plus background from the 2025 truce. The January end date and the 10% rate come from the web address, so check the full article before quoting. The diagram is conceptual and not drawn to scale. If the full Bloomberg article is supplied this record can be rewritten with its details. See also the 27 October item on the US-China port-fee truce.

items.title: How exposed is household wealth to an AI share crash?
items.summary: RBA research shows more household financial wealth is exposed to AI-related shares than in 2022, so the wealth effect of a share market fall on consumption is now about twice as large.
items.lede: RBA researchers Iris Chan and Marcus Miller estimate that 5.3% of household financial wealth was exposed to AI-related shares in June 2026, up from 2% at the end of 2022. A 30% fall in AI share prices would cut household financial wealth by only about 1.6%, but the effect on consumer spending would now be about twice as large as in 2022.
items.angle: Globalisation of financial markets means a sell-off on Wall Street can quickly reduce Australian household wealth through super funds and share portfolios. A crash would still hit only a small part of total wealth, but exposure has more than doubled since 2022, so the effect on consumption would now be about twice as large: AI shares fall, household wealth falls, the wealth effect cuts spending, aggregate demand falls and growth slows.
items.note: RBA research as reported by ABC News; the 1.6% is an estimate for a hypothetical 30% fall, not an outcome. Markets partly recovered on Friday and Monday after the 5 November sell-off. The bar chart and flow chart are illustrative.

items.title: Albanese wants backpacker rules in the UK free trade deal changed to help cut migration
items.summary: Shows how a free trade agreement can cover the movement of people, and the trade-offs of tighter working holiday rules for demand, housing and farm labour. Replaces the 2 November edition.
items.lede: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the working holiday arrangements in the Australia-UK Free Trade Agreement should change so that fewer people arrive and net overseas migration falls. British backpackers can currently stay up to three years without doing the specified work, such as regional farm work, that other working holiday makers must do.
items.angle: Migration affects both sides of the economy: it adds to aggregate demand (housing, consumption) and aggregate supply (labour). Cutting it may ease demand pressure but worsen labour shortages in farming, tourism and hospitality.
items.note: Replaces the 2 November item, whose figures are carried over. Any change needs the UK's agreement because the rules are part of a bilateral agreement. The Prime Minister described UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham as "very constructive". The diagram is the digest's illustration. UPDATE DUE: outcome of the talks.

items.title: Diesel squeeze: Australia pays more to find new suppliers
items.summary: A supply shock meeting inelastic demand: Australia imports almost as much diesel as before but pays far more, which worsens the terms of trade, widens the import bill and adds to cost-push inflation.
items.lede: Australia is the world's largest buyer of seaborne diesel, importing about 28 billion litres last year, and war in the Gulf and drone strikes on Russian refineries have redrawn the global diesel trade. Diesel peaked at A$3.20 a litre and is still about A$2.79, almost $1 higher than a year ago, with an extra $9 billion paid for imports between March and August.
items.angle: Higher import prices for fuel worsen Australia's terms of trade and add to the import bill in the current account. They also feed into cost-push inflation (Topic 3) and show a risk of globalisation: reliance on a few suppliers threatens fuel security. South Korean refiners still rely on Middle Eastern crude, so the diversification is only partial.
items.note: An analysis by an academic. The $9 billion is a Climate Council estimate and the Strait of Hormuz closure date (28 February) is as stated in the article. The supply and demand diagram is illustrative, not to scale. Replaces the earlier one-page digest of the same article.

items.title: US tech giants push for trade retaliation over Australia's news levy
items.summary: Shows how a trade agreement can constrain domestic policy and how trade is used as leverage in digital and services disputes.
items.lede: Meta, Google and other platforms claim Australia's News Bargaining Incentive breaches the Australia-US Free Trade Agreement, and their lobby group CCIA has asked US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer to investigate. The incentive makes big platforms strike deals with publishers or pay a levy of 2.5% of their Australian digital advertising revenue.
items.angle: Contrast the platforms' view (a discriminatory tax that breaches AUSFTA) with the government's (it funds public-interest journalism, a merit good, and is a domestic policy choice). Canada dropped its digital tax last year under similar US pressure.
items.note: The platforms' claims are the lobby group's, and the government's revenue figure is its forecast. Meta, TikTok and Microsoft did not negotiate with publishers; Google had some deals to offset its bill, as reported. UPDATE DUE: any US investigation.

items.title: RBA raises the cash rate to 4.85%: the factors the Board weighed
items.summary: A primary-source account of why the Monetary Policy Board raised the cash rate on 3 November: broad-based inflation, tighter capacity, energy prices and expectations, weighed against slowing growth, falling house prices and rising unemployment. Pages 3–4 link the decision to Topic 1: oil, international business cycle, financial flows and the exchange rate.
items.lede: On 3 November 2026 the RBA's Monetary Policy Board raised the cash rate target by 25 basis points to 4.85%, by six votes to three. The Statement on Monetary Policy says inflation is broadly based, capacity pressures are a little tighter than assessed in August, and the inflation outlook has been revised materially higher on fuel and other conflict-related costs.
items.angle: Use the decision to show how the Board weighs inflation, capacity and expectations against slowing growth, falling house prices and rising unemployment. Monetary policy works on demand and with a lag, so it answers an energy supply shock by slowing the whole economy. The 6–3 vote shows the judgement involved, and the Statement stresses uncertainty about the neutral rate and the NAIRU. Topic 1 link: Australia is a small open economy and a price taker, so world energy prices, partner growth and global interest rates reach domestic inflation and the cash rate; the exchange rate has not added tightening because other central banks also raised rates.
items.note: Based on primary sources: the RBA media release of 3 November 2026 and the November 2026 Statement on Monetary Policy (forecasts finalised 28 October). The 6–3 vote is from the media release; the three members who voted to hold are not identified in the material used, and the cautions listed in the digest are those the Statement sets out, not attributed to them. The cash rate chart shows the market-based path assumed in the forecasts, which was set before the decision. Market odds of a hike rose from about 20% to 60% after his 21 October speech and to 80% after the 28 October CPI.
items.angle: Communication is part of the transmission mechanism, but it creates a tension with board independence. Hauser says he followed the 2023 RBA Review's advice to explain policy publicly and wants the RBA to explain how it would react to new data without promising a path for rates.
items.note: The claim that board members felt pre-empted is reported, not confirmed by the RBA. Westpac's Luci Ellis and former board member Warwick McKibbin are quoted with opposing readings. Follows the 21 October Hauser and 26 October Hunter items.

items.title: Are there any good alternatives to raising interest rates?
items.summary: Asks whether anything beats a rate rise for cooling inflation, weighing temporary taxes and the super guarantee against the cash rate, with the transmission mechanism, time lags and weaker transmission this cycle.
items.lede: The RBA raised the cash rate from 4.60% to 4.85% on 3 November, its fifth rise this year and the highest since 2008, with three of the nine Board members wanting to hold. ABC money correspondent Jessica Irvine asks whether there is a better way to bring inflation down and concludes rate hikes are crude, but they are the tool we have.
items.angle: Use it to evaluate monetary policy: the transmission mechanism, time lags, limitations and the importance of credibility. Each step takes time and the effect depends on how indebted households are; lower debt-to-income and borrowers who kept repayments high after the 2025 cuts mean weaker transmission this time. Irvine compares rate hikes (an independent RBA can act quickly, but they are crude and hit mortgage holders hardest) with temporary taxes set by an independent body (which would spread the burden more widely, though no country uses this today) and adjusting the 12% super guarantee, which she says needs more investigation.
items.note: An analysis piece by a money correspondent, so the conclusion is her view. Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser said trust in the RBA's ability to bring inflation down soon has 'fallen materially'. Irvine argues deficits of about 1% of GDP are not a large stimulus, so they are not the main cause of inflation. The diagram is illustrative, not to scale. Replaces the earlier digest of the same article (it also cited the 2014 budget repair levy on incomes over $180,000). See also the 2 November item on spending cuts versus rate rises and the 7 November item on the December budget update.

items.title: Should the budget be tightened in December's update?
items.summary: Weighs the case for and against cutting spending in the December MYEFO while the RBA raises rates, and shows how tightening both policies would shift AD further left.
items.lede: With the RBA raising rates, some commentators want the government to cut spending in the December mid-year economic update, and ABC political editor Jacob Greber argues it is the right prescription at the wrong time. Minister Clare O'Neil has confirmed a savings package for the update that she called a 'mini budget', with priorities of lower spending, cost-of-living relief that does not add to inflation, and productivity.
items.angle: The policy mix matters: if fiscal and monetary policy both tighten into a slowdown, the combined effect on growth and jobs could be larger than intended. Higher rates already reduce consumption and investment, and spending cuts would reduce G as well, shifting AD from AD1 to AD2, so the price level eases but real GDP falls and unemployment rises. Case for cutting: spending is above pre-pandemic levels, it would help the RBA reduce inflation, and fiscal policy could share the load with mortgage holders. Case against (Greber): the deficit is already narrowing faster than forecast, the RBA expects business investment to collapse in the second half of 2027, and house prices have fallen more than Treasury expected.
items.note: The case against tightening is Greber's argument. Former RBA board member Warwick McKibbin told 7.30 this level of spending is not a problem while inflation and interest rates are low, and Governor Bullock says monetary policy cannot affect global oil prices so the RBA is targeting domestic capacity pressures. The savings package details are not yet known. The diagram is illustrative. UPDATE DUE: the December MYEFO. See also the 2 November item on spending cuts versus rate rises and the 5 November item on the budget versus inflation.
